paragraphs: After more than a decade, the call to free the last of the government’s lab chimpanzees has been answered.

This week, the National Institutes of Health announced that it is releasing its final group of research chimps to a 200-acre forested federal sanctuary in Keithville, Louisiana. Next year, the 33 primates will relocate from the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Texas to Chimp Haven, home of more than 250 chimps owned or supported by the NIH.

“We believe that chimpanzees should have the opportunity to engage in natural behaviors like you would see in the wild, so that includes climbing trees, foraging for different food items and interacting with other chimpanzees,” said Rana Smith, the sanctuary’s president and chief executive officer, whose residents range in age from 9 to almost 67 years old.

Chimp Haven, a retirement home with five-star amenities, last received 21 chimps from the Alamogordo Primate Facility in New Mexico in 2025, a decade after the government banned invasive testing on the endangered species. Before the ruling, Kathleen Conlee, vice president of animal research issues for Humane World for Animals, said the agency used the great apes in biomedical research, such as studies on AIDS and other infectious diseases.

The NIH has not yet disclosed the names, genders or ages of the chimps, but Smith said her staff has a full roster of activities planned for the newest members of the tribe, such as violin concerts, food puzzles and film screenings.
“We have chimps that enjoy watching movies,” she said. “They love Bollywood movies and musicals.”

paragraphs: SAN FRANCISCO — As Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei regaled investors last month with his artificial intelligence company’s plans for future products, a very different meeting unfolded elsewhere in the company’s headquarters.

Anthropic had invited more than a dozen academics, think tank fellows and media figures for briefings from senior staff on how society should navigate the rise of powerful AI. Guests were asked to first read an essay by Amodei that argued that AI was advancing dangerously fast, and the 23,000-word “constitution” that guides his company’s chatbot with statements like “Claude should not even tell white lies.”

In a 10th floor conference room down the hall from a built-in barista bar, attendees recalled, Anthropic staff described how AI was increasingly able to improve itself and that teaching machines morals might stop them from becoming harmful. “They feel it’s going to be a transformative event for humanity and society needs to be prepared,” said New York University economist Arpit Gupta, who joined the two-day program. “I got the sense that they’re not happy with the public discourse” about AI, he said, and want to change it.

Gupta and fellow guests received a crash course in the view from inside Anthropic, a company that Amodei has constructed around his vision that AI will soon accelerate beyond human intelligence and his beliefs about how to build it safely.

The company launched on the stock market Thursday, ending the week with a valuation of more than $1.5 trillion that transformed Amodei and his co-founders into deca-billionaires. He propelled Anthropic to the front of the AI race, reshaping the U.S. economy this year by winning over business clients to its technology — and through a unique corporate culture that attempts to reconcile the conflict between chasing profits and doing what’s best for society.

Amodei, a cerebral presence who doesn’t project the naked ambition of an archetypal Silicon Valley founder, leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as “Dario Vision Quests,” expounding on the company’s thinking around AI development, geopolitics and more while inviting employees to discuss and debate. The CEO’s output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China’s AI development, and Claude might be conscious.

Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world’s most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company’s ethos, including several current and former employees.

At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what’s best for the world. “It’s kind of [a] Manhattan Project-style, crazy, fun place, if you think it’s going to work out well,” said former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, publicly resigned in September, warning that Anthropic felt locked into an AI race that risked human extinction.

“A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We’re going to put on our capes and we’re going to be the responsible ones, and we’re going to accrue great power, but … because we’re doing it responsibly, it’s responsible to acquire more power,” said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company.
Anthropic’s leaders tightly control the details of the company’s internal debates through a zero-tolerance policy on leaks and strong social norms enforcing confidentiality, former employees said.

Anthropic launched an internal investigation last year after Wired reported that Amodei had acknowledged in a Slack message that accepting funding from Middle East states was likely to “enrich dictators,” said the former employee who left this year. The leaker was fired, the employee said, an incident that has not been previously reported. Details from Amodei’s copious Slack memos appear to have leaked only once more since.
Anthropic declined to comment.

The company suggested in its IPO prospectus that Anthropic’s revenue could reach about the size of the entire U.S. economy. Its message to investors fit with a vision of the future that Amodei often sketches out for his staff, people familiar with the company said, in which AI companies have the power of nation-states.

After nearly six years of telling his workers that powerful AI will force society’s leaders to make difficult decisions, Amodei is now one of the powers who must decide how to act, in a major test of the corporate culture he has created. “The moment the whole company was preparing for the whole time is now approaching,” an early Anthropic employee said.

Amodei was convinced of his vision long before he became a CEO with a flock to tend. After joining OpenAI as vice president of research in 2016, he used a laptop and printer kept physically disconnected — or “air gapped” — from the internet to work on essays about how to build more powerful AI, said Geoffrey Irving, who worked closely with Amodei in OpenAI’s research department.

“Dario was paranoid about some of the stuff being an ‘infohazard,’” said Irving, containing ideas that could lead to immense harm if they fell into the wrong hands — like the recipe for a nuclear bomb. Amodei also purchased air-gapped laptops for a couple of other employees, including Irving, he said.

Amodei’s writings on how to build more powerful AI caught on fast with other researchers at OpenAI. He has said in public remarks that he left because he lost trust that the company would handle disagreements over how to develop AI in good faith. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)
He set out to create a more safety-conscious culture when he co-founded Anthropic in 2021 with six people from his inner circle, most of them from OpenAI.

In an internal memo the following year, Amodei laid out the stakes. “The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there’s a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity,” he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show. He added that truly capable AI “seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons.”

Amodei was careful about those he hired to work on that existential challenge. Recruits were screened with a “culture interview,” even for back office and policy roles, according to former employees and an archived copy of the company’s careers page.

One prospective hire said they were quizzed in the culture interview about ideas featured in company reading material sent ahead of interviews with Anthropic this spring, including two of Amodei’s essays about good and bad future paths for AI.
It’s “a bit of an ‘are you ready for the cult’ interview,” an Anthropic hiring manager texted the unsuccessful candidate, according to a screenshot reviewed by The Post.

The talent that made it through that filter drew heavily from the Bay Area’s effective altruism community, whose members try to calculate and maximize the good they can do in the world. Amodei, an influential early member of that scene, played a role in shifting donors’ attention toward the risks of AI, according to planning documents posted online by a philanthropy where he was a technical adviser. (He has since distanced himself from the movement.)

In those Bay Area circles, working at Anthropic brought clout. “I noticed that I was cooler because I was there,” said a former engineer who joined in 2021. The burgeoning field of AI safety, which grew to include a network of nonprofit organizations and other groups, focused on preventing calamity from AI, placed its hopes in Amodei and his Ants as high-integrity people who recognized the technology’s potential harms.

As the company grew, Anthropic sidestepped the liberal workplace politics and culture-war debates that caused internal divisions at more conventional Silicon Valley firms, multiple former employees said.

At one of his early Vision Quest talks, Amodei declared himself a patriot, said the early employee, who summarized the CEO’s remarks as, “America is awesome, democracy needs to win, it’s okay to support the military.” In public and in private, former employees said, Amodei casts the global AI race as a contest between democratic and authoritarian countries, and takes a hard-line view of China, which he argues should be cut off from the powerful chips needed to develop AI systems.

Even after Amodei’s remarks about Middle Eastern funding leaked, he promised staff in a Vision Quest talk last year that he wouldn’t self-censor, according to the former employee who left the company this year.

“Dario made a point to say, ‘I’m not going to let these leaks deter me from being honest. I care too much about the internal culture, and I don’t want to let the internal culture degrade.’ And he said some very unfiltered things just to make a point,” including calling Nvidia’s then-CEO Jensen Huang greedy, the former employee said.

Anthropic has recently moved to seed Amodei’s ideas with opinion-makers outside the company, scheduling a series of convenings like the one Gupta attended at Anthropic’s offices last month. The discussions have been held under the Chatham House Rule, but guests are encouraged to share what they heard.
“A typical session will focus on capabilities and safety, interpretability, national security, Claude’s constitution, economics etc.,” according to a Google Form for the events viewed by The Post.

Amodei did not speak to Gupta’s group, but whenever the topic turned to China, he said, staffers reliably echoed the CEO’s calls for export controls in a way that reminded Gupta of how AI chatbots reflect the values of their developers.
but the economist said staffers reliably echoed the CEO’s strident public warnings about AI, in a similar way to how AI chatbots reflect the values of their developers.
Before ringing in Anthropic’s record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits.

“To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said.

His promise to go slow even as he placed his company’s fate in the hands of public shareholders echoed an essay he published in September, days after employee Coxon resigned and raised concerns about extinction risks, triggering uproar across Silicon Valley and in Washington.
Many Ants still at the company trust Amodei.

“They buy the narrative that leadership will work really hard and [are] not going to let the incentives steer them,” the former engineer said. After Anthropic’s IPO, about 600 employees own equity stakes worth more than $100 million, and more than 5,000 own shares worth more than $1 million, according to investment marketplace Hill.com.

For some in the AI safety community that has long seen Amodei as the industry’s only principled actor, the mismatch between his rhetoric and his company’s drive to make AI more powerful is no longer tenable.

Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI employee who has criticized the company’s safety practices since resigning in 2024, said that it was good that Amodei still writes out and circulates his ideas, but insufficient.

“It’s nice to be transparent. It’s nice to write more, ideally to the public,” but it doesn’t mean the public should trust the company or its leadership, said Kokotajlo, who along with Coxon spoke at a protest outside Anthropic’s headquarters the day its shares began to trade.

Irving, Amodei’s former collaborator at OpenAI, said that he now mostly skims the Anthropic CEO’s memos or reads summaries on Substack. “He’s just … another AI company CEO trapped in this horrible race,” he said.

The right thing for Anthropic to do is to stop pushing AI forward until the level of risk can be made acceptable, he said. Anthropic’s internal culture seems to have gotten the company to “a unified view that they should keep going,” he said, “and that’s just not a good view.”

A company called Celebration Cards pays Trump to use his name for the crypto venture.

paragraphs: As Asian stocks rallied over the decision by Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, nowhere were the celebrations more ebullient than in China and Taiwan, where tech leaders, investors and even street market vendors hailed the AI executive as a hometown hero on whom the success of the tech industry — and global markets — relies.

Huang’s reinstatement, under direct pressure from President Donald Trump, seemed to avert a short-term diplomatic crisis — Beijing had forcefully denied allegations that his paramour Alice Huang was a Chinese operative — but left open serious questions about the White House’s handling of serious espionage concerns and potential investigations by the Democratic Congress that is set to take office in January.
News of Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy seemed to do little to dim the adoration many across Asia had for him.

“The king is back!” read one headline by China’s state-affiliated financial news outlet Star Market Daily.

At least three Huang-related hashtags topped trends on the Chinese social media platform Weibo on Tuesday, as Japan’s Nikkei rose nearly 4 percent, Korea’s Kospi index gained more than 6 percent and Taiwan’s main stock market index gained nearly 9 percent.

“I’m so happy that [Huang] is making a comeback,” Duan Yongping, a Chinese American billionaire entrepreneur and value investor nicknamed the “Chinese Buffett,” posted on Xueqiu, a major Chinese investment social network and wealth management platform.
In the nearly two-week period of upheaval — from Huang’s resignation Nov. 12 to the board’s announcement Monday — people in Asia sent wishes for his return.

The message was particularly clear in Taiwan, where Huang was born before moving to the United States at age 9. Taipei 101, Taiwan’s tallest building, lit up with messages of support: “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” and “Thrive Together.” Representatives of Taiwan’s technology industry associations organized and funded the display.

At a temple to the matchmaker god Yue Lao in Taiwan’s Tainan, lanterns were lit for Huang to “cut off bad romantic relationships,” according to a local news station. The reason for this: “to save Taiwan’s stock market supply chain.”

On the other side of the world, Silicon Valley tech leaders including Elon Musk had also been backing Huang as the scandal unfolded. But his biggest cheerleader, it seemed, was Trump, who said he personally orchestrated the effort to reinstate Huang over the past several days.
Nvidia said in announcing Huang’s reinstatement that its board received input from “senior levels of the United States government.”

“The Trump administration’s intervention mattered enormously. If anything, it shows just how important Nvidia, and Huang at the center of it, have become to America’s AI ambitions,” said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.

Huang’s return is good news for China’s AI industry, given its dependence on Nvidia and the importance of American technology to Chinese models, Lee said. paragraphs: SHENZHEN, China — Sellers at Huaqiangbei market, a sprawling electronics bazaar, hawk smartwatches, consumer drones, motherboards — and cutting-edge Nvidia chips supposedly barred from China by the U.S. Commerce Department.

This open defiance of U.S. export controls is in evidence in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, just a few miles from the state villa where President Donald Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week and hailed him as a “friend.”
During a recent visit, one vendor in a corner of Huaqiangbei at first denied that he knew where to find high-end Nvidia chips. Then, he relented.
The day's top stories, curated by Washington Post editors. Sign up for free
After making a few calls to suppliers, he quoted a price of 20 million renminbi — around $3 million — for a server containing eight Blackwell B300s, the most advanced Nvidia chips produced.

The traders of Huaqiangbei form part of a vast effort in China to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States, which China lags in the artificial intelligence race. In recent weeks, that effort has only grown more urgent as the U.S. tightens its export controls following an alleged Chinese espionage plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced by his board to step down before a whiplash return on Monday.

In a sign that their supply networks are coming under strain from the fast-moving events in the U.S., Huaqiangbei vendors said that the prices of Nvidia chips have risen drastically in the past few weeks.

Two months ago, a Blackwell B300 server was priced at just $2 million, according to Wu, a vendor who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his last name for fear of official scrutiny. “If U.S. authorities or Nvidia restrict the supply, the price will rise,” Wu said. “But of course, after a certain point, the demand will be very low. It’s not good for our business.”

Nvidia does not publicly disclose prices for its high-end chips, but an equivalent B300 server retails for roughly $500,000 to $600,000 in the U.S., said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank.

The prices in Huaqiangbei, which fluctuate as market conditions change, illustrate a complex and ever-evolving battle between Beijing, Washington and Nvidia to widen or narrow the supply of U.S. chips available to China.
Nvidia chips are the “decisive factor” in the AI competition between the U.S. and China, Chan said. “Who can get access to the best Nvidia chips matters tremendously.”
Finding U.S.-restricted Nvidia chips to buy in Shenzhen is simply a matter of asking the right person.

Vendors across multiple buildings of Huaqiangbei market quoted prices of $3 million to $3.4 million for a single B300 server with eight graphics processing units, or GPUs. Development of a cutting-edge AI model can require tens of thousands of these B300 GPUs.
Since Nvidia introduced its Blackwell series of chips in 2024, the U.S. has banned their shipment to China over security concerns and a stated desire to protect the U.S. technological edge.

But in a sign of the Trump administration’s shaky approach to enforcement — including sporadic waivers of the rules — Blackwells are available in Shenzhen, along with other export-controlled Nvidia chips critical for developing the most advanced artificial intelligence models. It is not illegal under Chinese law for vendors to sell chips, regardless of U.S. law.

“If I ever wanted to be a big [Chinese AI developer] and I needed a bunch of Blackwells, I would just go to Huaqiangbei and work out a deal,” said Joshua Woodard, founder of the Sparrows, a Shenzhen-based supply chain consultancy.
The stalls tend to attract a mix of fledgling start-ups, independent developers and foreign customers, vendors said.
For the past four or five years, Russians and Iranians have come to buy Nvidia chips at Jason Cheng’s stall, he said.

“We don’t care which country a customer comes from, as long as they can pay,” said Cheng, who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his English name to avoid drawing the attention of authorities.

The Washington Post was not able to verify the authenticity of the proffered Blackwells, which are stored in off-site warehouses — some in Shenzhen, others in nearby Hong Kong, according to the vendors, who requested up-front deposits to view the chips in person.
One vendor, whom The Post contacted online, shared a photo of a sealed crate in a Shenzhen warehouse, saying that it contained Blackwell B300s.

Other chips were easier to track down. In his stall, Wu openly displayed what appeared to be Nvidia RTX 5090 chips and said he also had RTX PRO 6000 chips in stock. Both are significantly cheaper than the Blackwells but can be used in AI development and remain restricted for export from the U.S.

Wu’s chips are usually sourced from Hong Kong, he said, acknowledging their restricted status. “We’re not clear about where they are before Hong Kong. But the United States sells the 6000s to other countries in the world, don’t they?”

In an emailed statement, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, wrote: “China’s position on U.S. chip exports to China is consistent. China opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

Washington began cracking down on export control violations earlier this month in response to the revelation first reported by the New York Times that Nvidia’s Huang had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a customer of the company and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. (The two are not related.)

The affair set off alarms in Washington, but even during the 11-day period of Huang’s ouster from Nvidia, scrutiny around the California-based tech company continued. For U.S. policymakers, Huang’s affair broadened into a wider issue: “Whether Nvidia was either knowingly or unknowingly allowing for its chips to eventually be accessed by Chinese companies,” Chan said.
Most high-end Nvidia chips have been under U.S. export controls since 2022, but the products nevertheless have made their way into China, according to Trump administration officials.

China also made little effort to conceal that it was getting the chips. Procurement records for Chinese research institutes and universities, which are public, list acquisitions of export-restricted Nvidia chips through 2025 and 2026, including as recently as last month.
Nvidia has denied it knowingly defied bans to sell chips to China, though it carried out a years-long lobbying campaign in Washington to loosen the restrictions.
Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

In Washington, the flow of the chips was aided by disagreements within the Trump administration on how stringently to enforce the export controls, which fall under the purview of the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS).
This month, that infighting spilled into public view as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for turning a blind eye to Nvidia chips slipping into China.

Leadership was lacking “from day one,” said a former BIS official who served in the second Trump administration, speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. “There was no direction on what to do and no help on what to do.”

The former BIS official, along with another former senior administration official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive details, said enforcement was slowed by the stipulation that Jeffrey Kessler, the head of BIS, had to personally approve many routine actions. That included traveling overseas and contacting other parts of the U.S. government to investigate alleged violations, the former BIS official said. “Everything was having to go across his desk for an action to be taken. He has been hands on and gumming up the works for so much of this.”
The Commerce Department and BIS did not respond to requests for comment.

Uneven enforcement aside, the Commerce Department at times authorized the sale of restricted chips. Earlier this year, it approved a plan to sell nearly 580,000 export-controlled Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, two of which are linked to the country’s military, according to documents released last week by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
U.S. authorities have since pledged to tighten rules around export controls, including closing the loophole on Chinese firms “renting” the computing power of Nvidia chips stationed outside China.

But it remains to be seen whether Lutnick enforces the export controls, Chan said. “They might go along with the letter of the law, but are they going to go along with the spirit of the rule and really take it all the way?”

Lutnick and Nvidia now face a bipartisan reckoning in Washington. Democratic members of Congress and Trump administration officials alike have called for deeper scrutiny into Nvidia’s business practices and the Commerce Department’s handling of the scandal, with some Democrats urging Lutnick’s ouster.
For all their shaky implementation, U.S. export controls were monitored by Chinese officials with growing concern — and defiance.
“Experience has shown us that we cannot be choked by ‘chokeholds,’” Xi said in a speech last December, referring to Washington’s effort to halt China’s inflow of Nvidia chips.

But in Beijing, policymakers disagreed over whether Chinese companies should continue procuring Nvidia chips or whether the country should lean on homegrown chipmakers to reduce reliance on its chief geopolitical rival.

China’s Ministry of Commerce is generally believed to favor importing Nvidia chips, while the National Development and Reform Commission, a powerful macroeconomic planning body, seeks to build up domestic chipmaking capacity, Chan said.

The closest Nvidia competitor in China is tech juggernaut Huawei, which is behind the Ascend line of chips intended for use in AI model development. Huawei’s chips fall well short of Nvidia’s, however, and the latest Chinese AI models, including those released by DeepSeek, relied at least partially on Nvidia chips, analysts say.

“It’s a question right now about whether the really big models … can be trained on purely Huawei chips,” Chan said. Training a model entirely on domestic technology, he said, “would mark a huge milestone for China’s chip industry and AI industry.”

Meanwhile, China’s AI industry faces broader obstacles. Aside from difficulties in securing enough Nvidia chips to train new models, Chinese companies — many of which offer free access to their models — are still struggling to find ways to turn a profit.

Wu, the Shenzhen vendor, thought the scramble in China to snap up Nvidia chips was overblown. He said he knew U.S. AI companies have shaky financials — but unlike their Chinese counterparts, the Americans could buy Nvidia chips without a black-market markup and charge for user subscriptions. “If you use such high-end equipment, at such a high cost, to offer models for free, how long can you support this enterprise?” he said.
The Chinese AI industry “is in a very tough place,” Chan said. Its revenue is “just far, far lower than what you would see from OpenAI or Anthropic.”
(The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)
Still, amid the industry’s pessimism, Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday came as a bright spot for the vendors of Huaqiangbei.

“We all support Jensen Huang. He is a standard-bearer of Nvidia,” Cheng said. “When he was replaced, we were concerned that GPU prices would keep rising. Now that he is back, we have more confidence that GPU prices will stay relatively stable.”
Isaac Arnsdorf in Washington and Lyric Li in Seoul contributed to this report.

During a recent visit, one vendor in a corner of Huaqiangbei at first denied that he knew where to find high-end Nvidia chips. Then, he relented.

After making a few calls to suppliers, he quoted a price of 20 million renminbi — around $3 million — for a server containing eight Blackwell B300s, the most advanced Nvidia chips produced.

The traders of Huaqiangbei form part of a vast effort in China to secure vaunted Nvidia chips and keep up with the United States, which China lags in the artificial intelligence race. In recent weeks, that effort has only grown more urgent as the U.S. tightens its export controls following an alleged Chinese espionage plot targeting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced by his board to step down before a whiplash return on Monday.

In a sign that their supply networks are coming under strain from the fast-moving events in the U.S., Huaqiangbei vendors said that the prices of Nvidia chips have risen drastically in the past few weeks.

Two months ago, a Blackwell B300 server was priced at just $2 million, according to Wu, a vendor who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his last name for fear of official scrutiny. “If U.S. authorities or Nvidia restrict the supply, the price will rise,” Wu said. “But of course, after a certain point, the demand will be very low. It’s not good for our business.”

Nvidia does not publicly disclose prices for its high-end chips, but an equivalent B300 server retails for roughly $500,000 to $600,000 in the U.S., said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington think tank.

The prices in Huaqiangbei, which fluctuate as market conditions change, illustrate a complex and ever-evolving battle between Beijing, Washington and Nvidia to widen or narrow the supply of U.S. chips available to China.

Nvidia chips are the “decisive factor” in the AI competition between the U.S. and China, Chan said. “Who can get access to the best Nvidia chips matters tremendously.”

Finding U.S.-restricted Nvidia chips to buy in Shenzhen is simply a matter of asking the right person.

Vendors across multiple buildings of Huaqiangbei market quoted prices of $3 million to $3.4 million for a single B300 server with eight graphics processing units, or GPUs. Development of a cutting-edge AI model can require tens of thousands of these B300 GPUs.

Since Nvidia introduced its Blackwell series of chips in 2024, the U.S. has banned their shipment to China over security concerns and a stated desire to protect the U.S. technological edge.

But in a sign of the Trump administration’s shaky approach to enforcement — including sporadic waivers of the rules — Blackwells are available in Shenzhen, along with other export-controlled Nvidia chips critical for developing the most advanced artificial intelligence models. It is not illegal under Chinese law for vendors to sell chips, regardless of U.S. law.

“If I ever wanted to be a big [Chinese AI developer] and I needed a bunch of Blackwells, I would just go to Huaqiangbei and work out a deal,” said Joshua Woodard, founder of the Sparrows, a Shenzhen-based supply chain consultancy.

The stalls tend to attract a mix of fledgling start-ups, independent developers and foreign customers, vendors said.

For the past four or five years, Russians and Iranians have come to buy Nvidia chips at Jason Cheng’s stall, he said.

“We don’t care which country a customer comes from, as long as they can pay,” said Cheng, who spoke on the condition that he be identified only by his English name to avoid drawing the attention of authorities.

The Washington Post was not able to verify the authenticity of the proffered Blackwells, which are stored in off-site warehouses — some in Shenzhen, others in nearby Hong Kong, according to the vendors, who requested up-front deposits to view the chips in person.

One vendor, whom The Post contacted online, shared a photo of a sealed crate in a Shenzhen warehouse, saying that it contained Blackwell B300s.

Other chips were easier to track down. In his stall, Wu openly displayed what appeared to be Nvidia RTX 5090 chips and said he also had RTX PRO 6000 chips in stock. Both are significantly cheaper than the Blackwells but can be used in AI development and remain restricted for export from the U.S.

Wu’s chips are usually sourced from Hong Kong, he said, acknowledging their restricted status. “We’re not clear about where they are before Hong Kong. But the United States sells the 6000s to other countries in the world, don’t they?”

In an emailed statement, Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, wrote: “China’s position on U.S. chip exports to China is consistent. China opposes the U.S. overstretching the concept of national security and abusing export control measures, which disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains.”

Washington began cracking down on export control violations earlier this month in response to the revelation first reported by the New York Times that Nvidia’s Huang had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a customer of the company and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. (The two are not related.)

The affair set off alarms in Washington, but even during the 11-day period of Huang’s ouster from Nvidia, scrutiny around the California-based tech company continued. For U.S. policymakers, Huang’s affair broadened into a wider issue: “Whether Nvidia was either knowingly or unknowingly allowing for its chips to eventually be accessed by Chinese companies,” Chan said.

Most high-end Nvidia chips have been under U.S. export controls since 2022, but the products nevertheless have made their way into China, according to Trump administration officials.

China also made little effort to conceal that it was getting the chips. Procurement records for Chinese research institutes and universities, which are public, list acquisitions of export-restricted Nvidia chips through 2025 and 2026, including as recently as last month.

Nvidia has denied it knowingly defied bans to sell chips to China, though it carried out a years-long lobbying campaign in Washington to loosen the restrictions.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

In Washington, the flow of the chips was aided by disagreements within the Trump administration on how stringently to enforce the export controls, which fall under the purview of the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS).

This month, that infighting spilled into public view as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for turning a blind eye to Nvidia chips slipping into China.

Leadership was lacking “from day one,” said a former BIS official who served in the second Trump administration, speaking on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. “There was no direction on what to do and no help on what to do.”

The former BIS official, along with another former senior administration official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive details, said enforcement was slowed by the stipulation that Jeffrey Kessler, the head of BIS, had to personally approve many routine actions. That included traveling overseas and contacting other parts of the U.S. government to investigate alleged violations, the former BIS official said. “Everything was having to go across his desk for an action to be taken. He has been hands on and gumming up the works for so much of this.”

The Commerce Department and BIS did not respond to requests for comment.

U.S. authorities have since pledged to tighten rules around export controls, including closing the loophole on Chinese firms “renting” the computing power of Nvidia chips stationed outside China.

For all their shaky implementation, U.S. export controls were monitored by Chinese officials with growing concern — and defiance.

“Experience has shown us that we cannot be choked by ‘chokeholds,’” Xi said in a speech last December, referring to Washington’s effort to halt China’s inflow of Nvidia chips.

But in Beijing, policymakers disagreed over whether Chinese companies should continue procuring Nvidia chips or whether the country should lean on homegrown chipmakers to reduce reliance on its chief geopolitical rival.

China’s Ministry of Commerce is generally believed to favor importing Nvidia chips, while the National Development and Reform Commission, a powerful macroeconomic planning body, seeks to build up domestic chipmaking capacity, Chan said.

The closest Nvidia competitor in China is tech juggernaut Huawei, which is behind the Ascend line of chips intended for use in AI model development. Huawei’s chips fall well short of Nvidia’s, however, and the latest Chinese AI models, including those released by DeepSeek, relied at least partially on Nvidia chips, analysts say.

“It’s a question right now about whether the really big models … can be trained on purely Huawei chips,” Chan said. Training a model entirely on domestic technology, he said, “would mark a huge milestone for China’s chip industry and AI industry.”

Meanwhile, China’s AI industry faces broader obstacles. Aside from difficulties in securing enough Nvidia chips to train new models, Chinese companies — many of which offer free access to their models — are still struggling to find ways to turn a profit.

Wu, the Shenzhen vendor, thought the scramble in China to snap up Nvidia chips was overblown. He said he knew U.S. AI companies have shaky financials — but unlike their Chinese counterparts, the Americans could buy Nvidia chips without a black-market markup and charge for user subscriptions. “If you use such high-end equipment, at such a high cost, to offer models for free, how long can you support this enterprise?” he said.

The Chinese AI industry “is in a very tough place,” Chan said. Its revenue is “just far, far lower than what you would see from OpenAI or Anthropic.”
